Weather map symbols

The symbols used on the practice maps, matching Table 2.2, plus the colours used on television weather maps.

SymbolNameWhat it showsWeather it brings

Highs and lows

H High

  • Higher air pressure than surroundings
  • Air sinks and warms, so clouds rarely form
  • Usually clear and dry, light winds
  • Winds blow clockwise and outward

L Low

  • Lower air pressure than surroundings
  • Air rises and cools, forming clouds
  • Cloud, precipitation, often wind
  • Winds blow counterclockwise and inward

Directions are for the Northern Hemisphere. Average sea-level pressure is 101.3 kPa.

Reading a weather map

  1. Systems move west to east. Across Canada, highs, lows and fronts are carried eastward by the prevailing westerlies and steered by the jet stream. To forecast, look west.
  2. Isobar spacing tells wind speed. Close together: strong winds. Far apart: light winds.
  3. Read pressure from the isobar labels. A place between the 101.6 and 102.0 lines has a pressure between those values.
  4. Symbols point the way a front moves. Triangles and semicircles are on the side the front is heading toward.
  5. Precipitation type follows temperature. On the warm side of a front it may rain; on the cold side the same storm may bring snow, with mixed precipitation in between.
